title: Electronic Structure of Atoms - Chemistry - Stability
subject: Chemistry

questions.q: What is the anomalous ground-state electron configuration of Chromium ($Cr$, $Z=24$)?
questions.explain: Expected config is $4s^2 3d^4$, but an electron promotes from $4s$ to $3d$ to achieve a stable half-filled $d​$-subshell. Correct config: $[Ar] 4s^1 3d^5$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: What is the anomalous ground-state electron configuration of Copper ($Cu$, $Z=29$)?
questions.explain: Expected config is $4s^2 3d^9$, but an electron promotes from $4s$ to $3d$ to achieve a stable fully-filled $d​$-subshell. Correct config: $[Ar] 4s^1 3d^{10}$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Why do elements like Chromium and Copper exhibit anomalous electron configurations?
options: Because $d​$ orbitals are lower in energy than $s​$ orbitals in all cases.
Because half-filled ($d^5$) and fully-filled ($d^{10}$) subshells possess extra stability.
Because they violate the Pauli Exclusion Principle.
questions.explain: The specific stability associated with exactly half-filled or fully-filled subshells (due to exchange energy and symmetry) favors the $s^1 d^5$ and $s^1 d^{10}$ configurations over $s^2 d^4$ and $s^2 d^9$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Given the stability rules, what is the configuration for the Copper(I) ion, $Cu^+$?
questions.explain: Copper is $[Ar] 4s^1 3d^{10}$. To form the $+1$ ion, it loses the single $4s$ electron, leaving a stable filled $d​$ subshell: $[Ar] 3d^{10}$ (or $[Ar] 4s^0 3d^{10}$).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Molybdenum ($Mo$) is directly below Chromium on the periodic table. What is its likely ground-state valence configuration?
questions.explain: Since Molybdenum is in the same group as Chromium, it follows the same stability trend favoring a half-filled $d​$ subshell. Thus, it adopts the $5s^1 4d^5$ configuration.
